intro: Une barque sur l’océan, marked D’un rythme souple, is the third piece of Ravel’s Miroirs. A slow melody sits above arpeggios that grow from a ripple into large waves covering the whole keyboard.

sections.label: A · Melody over arpeggios, F♯ minor
sections.mNote: F♯ minor; slow notes in the treble over left-hand arpeggios.

sections.label: Link · Arpeggios descend into the bass
sections.mNote: The right hand rests while the left hand descends.

sections.label: B · Chromatic runs and a long crescendo
sections.mNote: Both hands eventually move across the keyboard.

sections.label: C · Melody marked très expressif
sections.mNote: The bass arpeggios slow beneath the melody.

sections.label: D · High repeated figure
sections.mNote: Three sharps return; left-hand melody below repeated notes.

sections.label: E · Tremolos in the lower register
sections.mNote: A right-hand tremolo plays over a rolling bass.

sections.label: A′ · Reprise of the opening figuration
sections.mNote: A brief reprise ends on a chord marked pppp.

cues.title: Opening, 6/8 and 2/4
cues.text: The marking is D’un rythme souple — très enveloppé de pédales (a supple rhythm, wrapped in pedal). The left hand plays rising and falling figures beneath slow, tied notes in the right. Ravel writes two metres together, 6/8 and 2/4.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), Une barque sur l’océan, opening page: paired 6/8 and 2/4 signatures, pedal instruction, arpeggios and tied upper notes. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs_DemetsEd.pdf, PDF p. 14.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication to Paul Sordes
cues.text: Ravel dedicated Une barque sur l’océan to Paul Sordes, a painter in his circle of friends, Les Apaches. Each of the five pieces in Miroirs carries the name of one of the Apaches.
cues.evidence: Arisa Tachi’s account of Miroirs identifies the five Apache dedications and Paul Sordes as a painter. https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329

cues.title: First crescendo to fortissimo
cues.text: Low bass notes begin a long crescendo. The right hand plays chromatic runs while the left strikes deep notes and rolled chords. Both hands then cover the full width of the keyboard, with quieter bars between the loud passages.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 17–19: one-beat sf bar, pp en dehors, crescendo and wide ff–fff runs. https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:IMSLP02693-Ravel-Miroirs_DemetsEd.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Phrase marked très expressif
cues.text: After the runs, a glissando leads into a phrase marked très expressif. The bass arpeggios move more slowly. The piano plays a long melodic line, and small surges still break through it.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 19: glissandi, the 2/4 continuation, très expressif and slower bass arpeggios.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Shakespeare and the title Miroirs
cues.text: Ravel explained the title Miroirs with a line from Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: “The eye sees not itself / But by reflection, by some other things.” In 1928 he accepted the label “impressionist” only by analogy.
cues.evidence: The Shakespeare line (Julius Caesar, act 1, scene 2) is in Ravel’s Esquisse autobiographique, in English in Orenstein, A Ravel Reader (2003), p. 35, as quoted by Kyle Fyr, Music Theory Online 26.4 (2020), paragraph 5: https://mtosmt.org/issues/mto.20.26.4/mto.20.26.4.fyr.html. The remark on impressionism “by analogy” is in the same text, published in La Revue musicale, December 1938, in English in Ruti Abramovitch, “Maurice Ravel’s Miroirs for Piano” (Indiana University, 2012): https://scholarworks.iu.edu/dspace/bitstream/handle/2022/15206/Abramovitch_Ruti_2012.pdf

cues.title: Section in three flats
cues.text: Three flats replace the opening’s three sharps. High tremolos marked pianissimo alternate with runs through both hands, marked fortissimo.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 21–22: three-flat signature, pp tremolos and ff–fff runs. The returning sweep is also identified in Arisa Tachi’s formal account: https://enc.piano.or.jp/en/musics/329
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return to three sharps
cues.text: The three-sharp signature returns. High in the right hand a quick figure circles, pianissimo and sans nuances, “without shading”. Below it the left hand plays an expressive melody that rises and falls on its own.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 22–23: restored three-sharp signature, pp sans nuances in the right hand and p expressif in the left.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Crescendo to full-keyboard sweep
cues.text: The high figure repeats while the notes beneath it thicken into chords. Ravel marks augmentez peu à peu. The hands spread apart again, and the figure runs into another sweep across the full keyboard.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 25–26: augmentez peu à peu, fuller chords, and ff–fff sweeps.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Cruise on the yacht Aimée, 1905
cues.text: From 2 June to the end of July 1905 Ravel cruised the canals of France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany on the yacht Aimée, owned by Alfred and Misia Edwards. The painter Pierre Bonnard was among the guests. Miroirs was first played in January 1906.
cues.evidence: Manuel Cornejo’s Maurice Ravel chronology (1905): the trip of nearly two months aboard the yacht Aimée of Alfred and Misia Edwards, with Cipa and Ida Godebski, Pierre Bonnard and Pierre Laprade, on the canals of France, Belgium, the Netherlands and Germany, from 2 June to about 29–31 July; première of Miroirs on 6 January 1906 (1906 entries): https://boleravel.fr/wp-content/uploads/RAVEL_Chronology_2018.pdf

cues.title: Tremolo in the bass register
cues.text: The writing moves into the lower register, with both staves in the bass clef. A right-hand tremolo sounds above rolling bass notes, and Ravel marks it très fondu — thoroughly blended.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 27: both staves in the bass clef, repeated figures and le trémolo très fondu.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Return of the opening figure
cues.text: The opening ripple returns beneath tied notes in the right hand, now for only a few phrases. The arpeggios rise and fall, and the piece ends on a rolled chord marked pppp.
cues.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 30: brief return of the opening figure and final rolled pppp chord.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Right hand rests, left hand continues
transitions.from: A · Melody over arpeggios, F♯ minor
transitions.to: Link · Arpeggios descend into the bass
transitions.how: The metre changes to 3/4, then to 2/4. The right-hand phrases grow shorter and give way to rests. The left hand continues alone, and its arpeggios descend further into the bass. The three-sharp key signature remains, and naturals alter the harmony.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 16: changes of metre, right-hand rests and descending bass arpeggios.

transitions.title: One-beat bar before the 3/4 runs
transitions.from: Link · Arpeggios descend into the bass
transitions.to: B · Chromatic runs and a long crescendo
transitions.how: A one-beat bar marked sforzando breaks off the low arpeggios. The metre changes to 3/4, and the right hand starts chromatic runs, pp en dehors. The left hand plays rolled chords and deep bass notes. A long crescendo follows, and the writing spreads across both hands.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 16–17: 1/4 sf bar, 3/4, pp en dehors and the following crescendo.

transitions.title: Glissando into the 2/4 section
transitions.from: B · Chromatic runs and a long crescendo
transitions.how: The runs shared between the hands diminuendo. A right-hand glissando crosses above low octaves in the bass, and the metre changes to 2/4. The melody, marked très expressif, is in long notes over slower arpeggios.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 19: diminuendo, glissando and très expressif continuation.

transitions.title: Key change from three sharps to three flats
transitions.how: At a double bar the key signature of three sharps gives way to three flats. In 3/4, high pianissimo tremolos sound above a rising left-hand arpeggio. The next sweep moves into common time at fortissimo, with both hands running down the keyboard and back up.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 21: new signature, 3/4 tremolo passage and common-time ff runs.

transitions.title: High repeating figure in the right hand
transitions.how: A short très expressif phrase follows the sweep. The key signature of three sharps returns, and the right hand climbs towards the top of the keyboard. Its quick notes form a repeating figure, marked pp sans nuances, above an expressive line in the left hand.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 22–23: expressive link, restored signature and the contrasting instructions for the two hands.

transitions.title: Right-hand tremolo moves into the bass
transitions.to: E · Tremolos in the lower register
transitions.how: The wide descending sweeps contract into repeated low figures. The right hand’s tremolo, now written in the bass clef, merges with the left hand’s rolling accompaniment. Ravel marks the passage le trémolo très fondu, and the dynamic level falls gradually.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF pp. 26–27: descending sweeps, bass-clef tremolo and blending instruction.

transitions.title: Low chords lead back to the opening
transitions.from: E · Tremolos in the lower register
transitions.to: A′ · Reprise of the opening figuration
transitions.how: Low repeated chords diminish beneath short upper phrases. A rising run takes the hands back to the opening’s F♯-minor arpeggios, now pianissimo. The right hand plays its tied notes above them again. A brief reprise follows, and then the final pppp chord.
transitions.evidence: Demets first edition (1906), PDF p. 30: low chords, rising link and return of the opening arpeggios.

composer.epithet: Composer of a ballet built from two tunes and a snare drum, and of a suite of dances dedicated to his war dead.
facts: Paris Conservatoire from 1889; Fauré for composition, André Gedalge for counterpoint
Ricardo Viñes · Maurice Delage · Tristan Klingsor · M. D. Calvocoressi
Le Belvédère, Montfort-l’Amaury, 1921–37; now a museum
Two operas, two piano concertos, ballets, songs, chamber and piano music; no symphony

quote.text: Does it never occur to these people that I may be artificial by nature?
quote.source: To M. D. Calvocoressi, recalled in his Musicians Gallery (1933)

composer.background:
Ravel’s father took his sons to factories to see the machinery, and his mother sang to them. Pierre-Joseph was a Swiss-born engineer; Marie Delouart was Basque and had grown up in Madrid. Maurice was born in Ciboure on 7 March 1875, and the family moved to Paris three months later. He went back to the Basque coast many times. Spain appears often in his music, in the plucked-guitar attacks of Alborada del gracioso, the habanera in the Rapsodie espagnole and the clocks of a Toledo clockmaker’s shop in L’heure espagnole.

He entered the Paris Conservatoire at fourteen, studied piano with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot and lost his place in 1895 for failing to win the required prizes. André Gedalge gave him counterpoint lessons from 1897, and in January 1898 he entered the composition class of Fauré. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, gave the first performances of Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit, pieces he could not have played himself with comparable command.
